title: Paper Airplane

jokes.text: Oh. Hey, champions. Good morning. Quarter finals in an hour, hope you got some sleep, because I'm going to be haunting your nightmares tonight.
jokes.setup: Dwight greets coworkers warmly before a paper airplane contest
jokes.punchline: His trash-talk is absurdly intense for something as trivial as a paper airplane competition
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight hyper-intensity applied to a trivial stakes situation. Character integration is high — only Dwight would frame a paper airplane contest as nightmare-haunting warfare. Solid opener but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I did. I got some really good sleep. Did you? Zzz...
jokes.setup: Dwight threatens to haunt nightmares
jokes.punchline: Jim responds with a cheerful confirmation and then mimes sleeping sounds, completely deflating Dwight's intimidation
jokes.explanation: Jim's classic deflation of Dwight's pomposity. The 'Zzz' is perfectly economical — he doesn't argue, just demonstrates the irrelevance of Dwight's threat. Strong character integration for both.

jokes.text: It's not so easy on the environment, if you know what I mean.
jokes.setup: The paper is described as the Cadillac of products
jokes.punchline: Oscar's sardonic environmental aside, delivered with the knowing 'if you know what I mean' as if he's sharing insider knowledge about paper
jokes.explanation: Consistent with Oscar's character as the office intellectual/buzzkill, but the joke is fairly thin. 'If you know what I mean' adds nothing — the point is self-evident.

jokes.text: It's practically made of plastic.
jokes.setup: Oscar makes a vague environmental complaint about the paper
jokes.punchline: Kevin cuts in with a literal-minded non-sequitur that may or may not be true but is delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Kevin's blunt literal follow-up to Oscar's vagueness is mildly funny through character contrast. Economy is good (four words), but the joke doesn't have much depth.

jokes.text: Some used skill. Others relied on showmanship. Others seemed not to comprehend what a paper airplane is.
jokes.setup: Dwight narrates the first round of the contest like a sports announcer
jokes.punchline: The third category — not comprehending what a paper airplane is — is an absurd escalation that punctures the self-importance of the framing
jokes.explanation: Well-structured list joke with a strong third beat. The escalation from 'skill' to 'showmanship' to 'doesn't understand what a paper airplane is' is a classic comedy rule-of-three with a genuinely absurd payoff. Dwight as pompous sports narrator adds flavor.

jokes.text: I think I left my glasses down here somewhere. Crossing through. Beep, beep. Ow! Ow! I didn't see you! You should have been yelling 'crossing!'
jokes.setup: Creed wanders through the paper airplane competition area looking for his glasses
jokes.punchline: He runs into someone and blames them for not yelling out, revealing he knew he couldn't see and walked through anyway
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Creed — obliviously creating danger for others while blaming them for it. The 'beep beep' as if he's a vehicle is a wonderfully strange touch. Strong character integration. His self-righteous complaint after walking into someone is the real punchline.

jokes.text: We are now down to an elite eight. Well, seven, and Toby.
jokes.setup: Dwight announces the remaining contestants in official sports-announce fashion
jokes.punchline: He immediately excludes Toby from the category of 'elite,' a personal dig wrapped in a procedural announcement
jokes.explanation: Crisp, efficient Dwight-on-Toby contempt. The structure is excellent: set up a grand category, then immediately carve out an exception as an insult. Economy is near-perfect. Quotable. The fact that Toby somehow made it to the elite eight makes the dig funnier.

jokes.text: 'Be careful of that beaker. It contains dangerous acid!' — it does not say 'dangerous' and there's no exclamation point.
jokes.setup: Andy is directing Clark in a chemical safety video and adds dramatic flair to a line
jokes.punchline: Clark pedantically corrects the script, exposing the gap between Andy's theatrical ambitions and the mundane reality of an industrial safety video
jokes.explanation: Good situational comedy — Andy's grandiosity colliding with the literal small stakes of what they're actually making. Clark's script-lawyering is a nice character beat for him as the straight-man intern.

jokes.text: Clark ad-libbing 'dangerous' and an exclamation point into dry chemical safety script; director corrects him
jokes.setup: Clark is shooting an industrial safety video and reads the script with embellishments
jokes.punchline: The director points out neither 'dangerous' nor an exclamation point appear in the script — Clark is just trying to make it dramatic
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy about delusional aspiring actor Clark. The specificity of the exclamation point correction is funny. Sets up the running gag of Clark's movie delusions well.

jokes.text: HRPDC Chemical Handling Protocols. It's going to be seen by tons of workers in the industrial chemical community, one of whom could have a cousin whose brother is Brad Pitt, and then boom! Next thing you know, I'm in Moneyballs 2.
jokes.setup: Andy explains why the chemical safety video is a big career opportunity
jokes.punchline: His logic chain from 'industrial worker' to 'cousin' to 'Brad Pitt's brother' to 'Moneyballs 2' is an escalating fantasy that culminates in a fake movie title
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Andy's delusional Hollywood fantasy is perfectly escalated: each step of the logic is more tenuous than the last, culminating in 'Moneyballs 2' (not 'Moneyball' — the wrong title for the fake sequel). The misnaming of the film is a brilliant additional layer of obliviousness. Strong character integration — this is quintessentially Andy Bernard's narcissistic magical thinking. Quotable and rewatch-worthy.

jokes.text: Andy? Go away! We're running lines. / You wanted to see the gooey eye. / Oh, yeah. All right, get over here. I'm so freaked out by things going into eyes.
jokes.setup: Clark dismisses Andy, then Andy reminds him he wanted to see Clark's contact lens trick
jokes.punchline: Andy's simultaneous disgust and fascination with 'the gooey eye' — his revulsion is intense and personal, foreshadowing his later refusal to do the eyewash scene
jokes.explanation: Works as setup for the running gag about Andy's eye phobia. The 'gooey eye' as a phrase is memorably gross. Rewatch value because it plants the seed for the payoff later.

jokes.text: 'And remember, do not attempt to extinguish a chemical fire with water. It will only exacerbate the flame. The dangerous flame.'
jokes.setup: They're filming the safety video; Clark reads a line, then Andy ad-libs 'the dangerous flame'
jokes.punchline: Andy keeps adding 'dangerous' to everything, mirroring his earlier unauthorized script change — he's not learning from the correction
jokes.explanation: Nice callback to the earlier script correction — Andy literally cannot stop adding 'dangerous.' Shows he's learned nothing and the running gag has good internal logic.

jokes.text: Wait, wait, wait, wait. Stop, stop, stop. Don't go anywhere. I just need to find more colors. Let's do it six more times.
jokes.setup: The director signals they're done after one take
jokes.punchline: Andy insists on doing it 'six more times' and needs to find 'more colors' — revealing he has no idea how directing or acting works and is overcomplicating a simple industrial video
jokes.explanation: Andy's delusion about the artistry of a safety video is consistent character comedy. 'Find more colors' is the funniest beat — a meaningless director-sounding phrase that means nothing.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's couples therapy homework: forced 'acknowledge and appreciate' language in mundane conversation about tea
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam explain they have couples therapy homework to 'acknowledge and appreciate' each other's sacrifices
jokes.punchline: Pam says 'I acknowledge and appreciate that you went out of your way to get me tea'; Jim immediately undermines it by noting it wasn't out of his way at all
jokes.explanation: Smart setup for a running gag that pays off throughout the episode. The joke is that therapy-speak, meant to bridge connection, immediately becomes a vehicle for passive honesty ('it wasn't out of the way, I felt like tea anyway'). This is very Jim — his compulsive honesty undermines the therapeutic goal. Character integration is excellent.

jokes.text: And we are also supposed to speak our truths. Mmm-hmm. Because if I had spoken my truth earlier about not wanting to move to Philly, then maybe we wouldn't have had this opportunity for couples therapy.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam explain their therapy homework about 'speaking truths'
jokes.punchline: Pam (or Jim) uses 'opportunity' sarcastically for couples therapy — they've already absorbed the therapy language and are immediately weaponizing it with irony
jokes.explanation: The therapy-speak being immediately turned into a passive-aggressive tool is sharp. Calling couples therapy an 'opportunity' is a perfect ironic misuse of the framing they were just taught.

jokes.text: Carla Fern got me a gig. Hey. Yeah. Who's Carla Fern? Who is Carla Fern? Well... Wow. Uh, she's my agent and my drill sergeant. And one of my best friends.
jokes.setup: Andy announces his agent got him a gig; Oscar asks who Carla Fern is
jokes.punchline: Andy's exasperated 'Who is Carla Fern?' — incredulous that Oscar doesn't know — followed by the overly intimate description of someone the audience (and Oscar) has never heard of
jokes.explanation: Andy's delusion of celebrity is well-served here — he treats Carla Fern like everyone should know her, then describes her in increasingly personal terms. The 'Wow' reaction beat (presumably a look to camera) is implied.

jokes.text: Andy announces his agent 'Carla Fern'; Oscar asks 'Who's Carla Fern?' — Andy is scandalized
jokes.setup: Andy breathlessly announces Carla Fern got him a gig and references her as if she's a major industry name
jokes.punchline: Oscar's simple 'Who is Carla Fern?' deflates Andy's excitement; Andy responds with 'Wow' before explaining she's his agent, drill sergeant, and 'one of my best friends'
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy. Andy's delusions of show-business grandeur are undercut by nobody knowing his agent. The 'one of my best friends' tag reveals the sadness underneath — Carla is probably not a close friend at all. The escalating description (agent + drill sergeant + best friend) is nice.

jokes.text: And, Oscar, I already figured out if I have to get emotional in the film, I'm just gonna think about you getting dumped by the Senator. / Why don't you use your own life? Erin just dumped you. / It's a little raw. Not cool, Oscar.
jokes.setup: Andy shares his method-acting strategy of thinking about Oscar's personal heartbreak
jokes.punchline: Oscar points out Andy himself was recently dumped; Andy's wounded 'it's a little raw' reveals his total lack of self-awareness about using others' pain while protecting his own
jokes.explanation: Sharp cringe comedy. Andy's hypocrisy is exposed in real time — he's exploiting Oscar's pain as an acting resource while being totally blind to his own identical situation. Oscar's comeback is perfectly calibrated. 'It's a little raw. Not cool, Oscar.' is great character work — Andy is wounded but still trying to hold the moral high ground.

jokes.text: Not one of us remembers you saying anything about $2,000. / I forgot. I completely forgot.
jokes.setup: The office confronts Nellie about failing to mention the prize money
jokes.punchline: Nellie simply admits she forgot — no defensiveness, no excuse, just total ownership of an absurd oversight involving $2,000
jokes.explanation: Nellie's breezy admission is funnier than any excuse would be. The economy is excellent — 'I forgot. I completely forgot.' lands better than a longer explanation. It's very Nellie.

jokes.text: But at least now that large piece of cardboard that man was carrying around makes sense.
jokes.setup: The $2,000 prize is revealed and the office reacts
jokes.punchline: Jim's aside that a previously unexplained visual — someone carrying a large piece of cardboard — now makes sense, delivered to camera
jokes.explanation: A classic Jim-to-camera moment. The visual gag of someone walking around with an inexplicable large piece of cardboard (presumably to build a better paper airplane) is funny, and Jim's deadpan retroactive acknowledgment of it is well-timed. The understated delivery ('at least now...makes sense') is characteristic and effective.

jokes.text: I mean, sure, times are leaner now that I'm separated from the Senator. But my new studio apartment...is just fine for me and Phillip and Tinkie and Crinklepuss and Bandit Two and Pawlick Baggins and Lady Aragorn and their 10 kittens.
jokes.setup: Nellie downplays her financial situation after the prize money reveal
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of cats — with increasingly absurd names culminating in Tolkien references and 10 kittens — demolishes her claim that everything is 'just fine'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: Nellie insists she's fine, then the escalating cat list destroys that claim. The names are individually funny ('Crinklepuss,' 'Bandit Two' implying a deceased Bandit One, 'Pawlick Baggins,' 'Lady Aragorn') and the escalation to 10 kittens is devastating. 'Bandit Two' quietly implies tragedy. 'Pawlick Baggins' and 'Lady Aragorn' demonstrate Nellie's chaotic creativity. This joke earns its length through each name being individually funny. Quotable, rewatchable.

jokes.text: I had a chance with Dwight, but I didn't take it. And if I went back now, when I'm broke and he just inherited a farm, I'd be one of those gold-digging tramps you read about that try to bag a farmer.
jokes.setup: Angela talks to camera about her situation following her separation
jokes.punchline: The phrase 'gold-digging tramps who try to bag a farmer' is an absurdly specific category of social pariah, delivered with Angela's characteristic prim self-righteousness
jokes.explanation: Angela's prim moralism applied to herself — she'd rather suffer in poverty than be seen as a 'gold-digging tramp who bags a farmer,' a category she invented and is clearly preoccupied with. The specificity of 'bag a farmer' is very funny. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I'm with Esther now, she's younger than Angela. Sturdier, more comfortable with the scent of a manured field. Let's be honest, when it came to manured fields, Angela was, at best, indifferent.
jokes.setup: Dwight talks to camera about Angela's situation and his current girlfriend Esther
jokes.punchline: 'At best, indifferent' to manured fields is the most Dwight-specific romantic complaint in television history — his criteria for an ideal partner involve genuine enthusiasm for farm smells
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best standalone joke. 'At best, indifferent' to manured fields as a genuine romantic dealbreaker is extraordinarily specific to Dwight's character. No other character on any other show could deliver this line. The deadpan framing ('let's be honest') makes it even better — Dwight treating this as an objective assessment everyone should agree with. Highly quotable, perfect character integration, excellent economy. Comparable to an 8-range anchor joke.

jokes.text: Oh, wide wings, interesting. Hey! Why don't you back off? I mean, best of luck to you in the competition.
jokes.setup: Erin catches herself being aggressively competitive while examining an opponent's paper airplane
jokes.punchline: She starts with genuine menace ('back off'), then immediately catches herself and performs sweetness — the mask slipping and being replaced in real time
jokes.explanation: Good Erin character moment — her orphanage-honed aggression breaking through her cheerful exterior. The self-correction mid-sentence is funny and character-specific.

jokes.text: Growing up in an orphanage, you have to fight other kids for everything. Snacks, pillows, parents. I once ripped Greedy Susan's pigtail right off her head just for a handful of Crispix.
jokes.setup: Erin explains her competitive nature via her orphanage upbringing
jokes.punchline: 'Parents' is the dark pivot in the list; 'Greedy Susan' and 'Crispix' escalate the absurdity — she named her rival and remembers the specific cereal brand
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The list 'snacks, pillows, parents' is a perfect dark escalation — parents are not an item you normally fight over, making it a genuinely dark subversive beat that still lands as comedy because Erin's delivery is so matter-of-fact. 'Greedy Susan' is a perfect name (the irony of a child having such a specific adult-sounding nickname). 'A handful of Crispix' — not 'cereal,' specifically Crispix — is a brilliant specificity choice. This is among the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Are you in that paper documentary, too? Yup. You need an agent? No. I mean, you never acted in anything before. He's just my entourage. I was in The Wiz in high school.
jokes.setup: Andy's agent tries to recruit Darryl
jokes.punchline: Darryl deflects with 'he's just my entourage,' which is both an insult and a casual dismissal; Andy's retort about The Wiz is a genuinely earnest credential that makes it worse
jokes.explanation: Solid character beat. Darryl reducing Andy to 'entourage' status while Andy asserts a high school musical credential is good — the gap between Andy's self-image and reality is well-illustrated.

jokes.text: That's the clicky-clacker. He clicks that, and then the guy says, 'Action.'
jokes.setup: Andy is showing Darryl around the film set
jokes.punchline: Andy refers to the clapperboard as 'the clicky-clacker' — demonstrating he doesn't know the name of one of the most basic pieces of film equipment despite fancying himself a filmmaker/actor
jokes.explanation: 'The clicky-clacker' is a great character joke — Andy has absorbed enough movie-set atmosphere to be excited about the equipment but not enough to know its name. The childlike term perfectly encapsulates his cosplay of being a film industry professional.

jokes.text: We just need a picture of the top of your head in case we burn some of your hair off.
jokes.setup: Someone asks to take a picture of Darryl for the chemical safety video
jokes.punchline: The casual explanation that they might burn his hair off — stated as a matter-of-fact production concern rather than a safety issue — is a darkly funny bureaucratic moment
jokes.explanation: Dark little joke — treating potential hair-burning as a documentary/legal formality rather than a concern. The deadpan delivery implied by the context makes it land.

jokes.text: The 'actor' being photographed for hair-burning safety reference photo reacts awkwardly to the camera
jokes.setup: Someone needs a photo of the top of Andy's head in case they burn his hair in the chemical video
jokes.punchline: The whole situation — needing a pre-burn hair reference — implies real danger on what is supposed to be a mundane safety video set; Andy's awkward compliance adds to the absurdity
jokes.explanation: The premise — pre-burn hair documentation — is funny and absurd, but the joke isn't crisply delivered in the transcript. The implication is there but the execution is diffuse.

jokes.text: Kevin versus Angela matchup introduced; Kevin admits he bought a pre-folded plane off Craigslist
jokes.setup: Kevin is complimenting Angela's plane and says 'of course you made that yourself, because it's in the rules that you have to fold your own plane'
jokes.punchline: Asked if he made his own, Kevin answers 'Yes. In a way.' from one he bought on Craigslist
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Kevin joke. 'Yes. In a way.' is the ideal Kevin hedge — technically a lie but delivered with complete sincerity. Buying a pre-folded paper airplane on Craigslist is so specifically Kevin that it couldn't be anyone else. The structure is excellent: Kevin himself sets up the rules about self-folding, then immediately violates them. Self-implicating, oblivious, specific.

jokes.text: Nellie announces: 'I give you Toby and Angela' — described as 'two creatures, great and small'
jokes.setup: Nellie is announcing the next quarterfinal matchup
jokes.punchline: 'Two creatures, great and small' is a backhanded framing — it's the title of a beloved animal show/book — applied to two people in an office paper airplane contest, with the implication that their smallness (in stature and dignity) is what makes it apt
jokes.explanation: Nellie's phrasing has an entertainingly condescending quality. The 'All Creatures Great and Small' reference works as a mild joke about the pair's combined dignity deficit. Solid.

jokes.text: Hey, that is a really nice plane. You make that yourself? Uh-huh. Well, what am I thinking? Of course you made that yourself, 'cause it's in the rules that you have to fold your own plane. Kevin, did you make that yourself? Yes. In a way. From one that I bought on Craigslist.
jokes.setup: Dwight compliments a plane then catches himself, noting the rules require self-folding; he then asks Kevin directly
jokes.punchline: 'Yes. In a way. From one that I bought on Craigslist.' — Kevin has purchased a pre-folded paper airplane on Craigslist and is claiming authorship
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The buildup is patient — Dwight asks the seemingly rhetorical question, then has to ask Kevin specifically, and the three-part answer ('Yes. In a way. From one that I bought on Craigslist.') is perfectly structured. Each beat escalates: 'yes' (pause), 'in a way' (pause), then the full absurdity. The specificity of Craigslist as the paper airplane marketplace is inspired — Kevin found someone selling a folded paper airplane and purchased it. This is high-quality Kevin character work.

jokes.text: This is flatter. It's a piece of paper. You fold it into an airplane. Okay, that's enough. This is the end of the ream now. You have to pick one. I can't. I love them all too much. And none of them fly. So that makes it harder.
jokes.setup: Kevin is forced to make a new plane after the Craigslist one is disqualified
jokes.punchline: Kevin cannot choose among his planes because he loves them all — and none of them fly, which he treats as a secondary and only mildly relevant consideration
jokes.explanation: Kevin loving planes he admits don't fly is perfectly absurd and character-specific. 'So that makes it harder' as an afterthought — the inability to fly being a secondary concern to his emotional attachment — is brilliant Kevin logic. Very strong character integration.

jokes.text: Like Wilbur and Orville Redenbacher.
jokes.setup: Kevin vows to keep making planes until one flies, like the Wright Brothers
jokes.punchline: He conflates 'Wright' with 'Orville Redenbacher,' the popcorn brand founder, merging the Wright Brothers with a snack food mogul into one person
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single funniest line. The malapropism is perfect: Kevin knows something about the Wright Brothers (first names Wilbur and Orville), but 'Orville' triggers 'Redenbacher' (the popcorn guy), creating a hybrid figure who pioneered aviation AND popcorn. The commitment to saying 'Orville Redenbacher' with no awareness of the error is what makes it. It's the most Kevin thing Kevin has ever said — confident, wrong, unreflective, and perfectly economical. Highly quotable, widely referenced, and quintessential Kevin character comedy.

jokes.text: An Earl Grey tea for the lady. Oh, thank you. Um... I acknowledge and appreciate that you went out of your way to get me tea.
jokes.setup: Jim brings Pam tea as a nice gesture
jokes.punchline: Pam uses the stilted therapy language to acknowledge it — the therapeutic framing makes a simple kind act feel weirdly clinical and formal
jokes.explanation: The therapy-speak running gag continues. Functional callback, but not as sharp as the earlier deployment. The awkwardness of the formality over something small is the joke.

jokes.text: But, to speak my truth, it wasn't out of the way, because I felt like a tea anyway, so one trip.
jokes.setup: Pam formally acknowledges Jim going out of his way for tea
jokes.punchline: Jim uses the therapy language to correct the record — he didn't sacrifice anything, he was getting tea anyway
jokes.explanation: Good use of the therapy language as a tool for hyper-literal honesty — Jim weaponizes it for a minor pedantic correction. 'So one trip' as the punchline is economical and funny.

jokes.text: Well, to speak my truth, I switched to coffee in March. There's a new espresso machine. But I still acknowledge and appreciate the gesture.
jokes.setup: Jim has brought Pam Earl Grey tea; they're doing therapy-speak honesty
jokes.punchline: Pam reveals she doesn't even drink tea anymore — so both the gesture AND the effortlessness of the gesture are moot — but she'll formally acknowledge it anyway
jokes.explanation: Nice escalation of the therapy-speak gag — Jim's minimal gesture wasn't even the right gesture. The running gag peaks here momentarily. The formal acknowledgment of a completely useless gift is a good beat.

jokes.text: Okay, um, stop. Um, why are you smiling? I just made a character choice to be a scientist who really likes what he does and enjoys his job.
jokes.setup: Andy directs Clark in the safety video; Clark delivers his line while broadly grinning
jokes.punchline: Clark has decided the character of 'generic safety video actor' has a rich inner life — a joyful scientist who loves chemistry — which is not what's needed for a rote industrial video
jokes.explanation: Clark's method-acting delusion mirrors Andy's earlier grandiosity — both are taking an industrial safety video extremely seriously as an artistic vehicle. The irony of the student outpacing the teacher in pretension is well-played.

jokes.text: Yeah! Oh, eat it, piggy! Eat it! Oink, oink, oink.
jokes.setup: Erin beats Pete/Clark in a paper airplane round
jokes.punchline: Her victory celebration is aggressively degrading — calling a coworker 'piggy' and oinking at them — completely disproportionate to a paper airplane contest
jokes.explanation: Payoff for the orphanage aggression setup. The 'oink, oink, oink' is unhinged in the best way — the kind of trash talk you'd expect in a prison yard, not a paper airplane contest. Good callback to her dark competitive nature.

jokes.text: We still got to work together, so we should keep it civil. / I can't hear what you said. / You get your slop?
jokes.setup: Pete tries to de-escalate Erin's aggressive victory celebration
jokes.punchline: Erin literally can't hear him over her own triumph; then follows up with 'You get your slop?' — continuing the pig metaphor
jokes.explanation: Extending the pig gag with 'You get your slop?' is a solid extension. Pete's reasonable peacemaking being completely ignored adds to the cringe comedy.

jokes.text: You can do it, baby. / No, you can't, baby. You're gonna choke.
jokes.setup: Bob Vance encourages Phyllis before her match against Dwight
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately undercuts the spousal support by addressing Phyllis as 'baby' himself and predicting her failure in the same intimate register
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy joke. The mirroring of 'baby' — Bob using it as genuine affection, Dwight appropriating it for trash talk in the same breath — is very funny. 'You're gonna choke' delivered with the same intimate warmth is perfectly absurd.

jokes.text: Yeah, I plucked the chickens extra fast, 'cause I knew I was seeing you tonight. So there might just be a little bit of feather in your nuggets or just a little bit of meat inside of your pillow.
jokes.setup: Esther arrives early to see Dwight and explains why
jokes.punchline: She rushed the chicken-plucking, which means either feathers in the food or meat in the pillow — she presents this as a romantic gesture while describing potential food/comfort contamination
jokes.explanation: Delightfully specific farm-world joke. The idea that rushing chicken plucking creates two equally unpleasant outcomes (feathers in nuggets, meat in pillows), presented as romantic context, is absurdly charming. Esther is a good comic foil for Dwight precisely because she inhabits his world completely.

jokes.text: Esther shows up early because she 'plucked the chickens extra fast'; there might be feather in the nuggets OR meat in the pillow
jokes.setup: Esther surprises Dwight by arriving early to the competition
jokes.punchline: She plucked chickens quickly so as not to be late, meaning 'there might just be a little bit of feather in your nuggets or a little bit of meat inside your pillow'
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure — feather in nuggets / meat in pillow — is the joke, and it's well-executed. The cross-contamination of farm products into domestic items (and vice versa) is absurdly specific and implies a whole lifestyle. Dwight's pleased response ('I like a little feather in my nuggets') seals it. Very specific Scranton farm world-building.

jokes.text: All right, ladies and gentlemen, we are now down to the final four. Dwight, Erin, Angela, and God only knows how, but Toby.
jokes.setup: Dwight announces the final four contestants
jokes.punchline: 'God only knows how, but Toby' — escalating on the earlier 'well, seven and Toby' joke with renewed disbelief
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Dwight's contempt for Toby is a reliable well. The escalation from 'seven, and Toby' to 'God only knows how, but Toby' deepens the joke. The implication that Toby's advancement is inexplicable and possibly supernatural is a nice touch.

jokes.text: I'll get nude if you want me to. I'll go full Lena Dunham, but I... Dude, we don't need you to go nude, okay? Absolutely not.
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to find alternatives to putting water in his eye for the safety video
jokes.punchline: Andy offers full nudity as a counter-proposal to eyewashing — a completely unrelated and escalating alternative that references Lena Dunham's willingness to appear nude on Girls
jokes.explanation: Andy's negotiation strategy of offering nudity instead of eye contact with water is wonderfully absurd. The Lena Dunham reference is era-specific (Girls was current) and lands because Andy is genuinely offering this as a reasonable trade. Clark's horrified rejection is the perfect straight-man response.

jokes.text: Darryl, what do I do? Hold up, I'm looking at my spit in the microscope.
jokes.setup: Andy appeals to Darryl for help with the eyewash standoff
jokes.punchline: Darryl is completely uninterested in the crisis because he's examining his own saliva under a microscope — a perfectly specific and weird thing to be doing
jokes.explanation: Great Darryl moment. 'I'm looking at my spit in the microscope' is a beautifully specific reason to be unavailable. The total disengagement from Andy's crisis in favor of amateur saliva microscopy is perfectly Darryl — intellectually curious in random directions, completely unbothered by others' problems.

jokes.text: They want me to use real water in the eyewash scene. / So? / I can't squirt stuff in my eyeball. I've never even used an eyedropper.
jokes.setup: Andy explains his objection to the eyewash scene
jokes.punchline: 'I've never even used an eyedropper' — Andy's stated inexperience with eye drops as a reason he can't do a safety demonstration is both absurd and pathetically earnest
jokes.explanation: Andy's defense of his position reaches a new low — not 'I'm afraid' but 'I've never used an eyedropper,' as if this is a skill requirement he lacks. Earnest and specific in a character-consistent way.

jokes.text: It is time for a little T and A. I give you Toby and Angela.
jokes.setup: Dwight announces the next matchup
jokes.punchline: He sets up 'T and A' as a racy double entendre, then reveals it stands for 'Toby and Angela' — a deliberately anti-climactic but self-aware misdirection
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection/wordplay. The setup is knowing — Dwight is clearly aware of the double meaning — and the reveal is satisfying in its deliberate anti-eroticism. 'I give you Toby and Angela' as the least sexy possible resolution to 'T and A' is well-executed.

jokes.text: Is there a reason that we're excited for that little woman? / Yes, I pity her. She was recently in a situation where she could have had it all, and instead she lost everything. / Mmm. Is she a gambler? / In a way, but not in a stand-up-and-cheer kind of way, like the song.
jokes.setup: Robert from WeyerHammer asks Nellie why everyone is rooting for Angela
jokes.punchline: Nellie's description of Angela's situation is so vague and tragic that Robert's best guess is 'is she a gambler?' — and Nellie's clarification ('in a way, but not in a stand-up-and-cheer kind of way') is both accurate and absurd
jokes.explanation: Good exchange. The outsider perspective of Robert asking about Angela is a good device. 'Is she a gambler?' is a wonderfully specific wrong guess, and Nellie's clarification ('in a way, but not in a stand-up-and-cheer kind of way') is a solid line — the reference to the Kenny Rogers song 'The Gambler' adds a layer.

jokes.text: Andy, if you don't stick your eyes in that machine, I'm gonna call every production in Northeastern Pennsylvania. You won't even make an appearance on a security camera!
jokes.setup: Andy's agent (Carla Fern) confronts him about refusing the eyewash scene
jokes.punchline: 'You won't even make an appearance on a security camera' — the threat escalates from not getting roles to being invisible even on surveillance footage, which is both specific and ridiculous
jokes.explanation: Excellent line. The threat escalates from 'no productions' (professional death) to 'no security camera appearances' (literal non-existence in recorded media), which is a hilariously specific rock bottom. 'Northeastern Pennsylvania' grounds it perfectly — this is already a small market. The line is sharp, well-structured, and quotable. One of the episode's better jokes.

jokes.text: She yelled at me. [Andy crying in talking head]
jokes.setup: Carla Fern has just aggressively threatened Andy's career
jokes.punchline: Andy's talking-head confession is simply 'she yelled at me' — delivered through tears, reducing a grown man's breakdown to the complaint of a scolded child
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words capture Andy's total emotional regression. The talking head context (he went to cry in an interview room) makes it funnier. The simplicity of the complaint against the dramatic lead-up is the joke.

jokes.text: Andy talks himself into doing the eyewash scene by creating an alter ego: 'Older Male Lab Assistant Number One'
jokes.setup: Andy can't psychologically bring himself to use the eyewash machine as himself
jokes.punchline: He creates 'Older Male Lab Assistant Number One' — the character's full screen-credit name — as a persona who can do it; asks if people believe in this character
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Andy gives himself a full acting character to psychologically separate himself from the act of using an eyewash station. The character's name is his literal screen credit — 'Older Male Lab Assistant Number One' — which is both a specific industry detail and the saddest possible acting role. 'Do you believe in me? I believe in me.' is a great delivery beat.

jokes.text: I can't wash my eyeball. I can't do that. I can't. Andy Bernard can't squirt water in his eye and act like it doesn't freak him out. But you know who can? Older Male Lab Assistant Number One.
jokes.setup: Andy is still refusing to do the eyewash scene
jokes.punchline: He creates a fictional character ('Older Male Lab Assistant Number One') who can do things Andy Bernard cannot — essentially method-acting in reverse by inventing an alias to perform a basic task
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Andy jokes. The logic is impeccable from an absurdist standpoint: Andy can't do it as himself, so he invents a character — 'Older Male Lab Assistant Number One,' a name so generic it's clearly just a safety video role — who can. He's method-acting to wash his own eyes. The specificity of 'Number One' (implying there might be a Number Two) is the perfect detail. Strong character integration — this is exactly how Andy's narcissism and fragility intersect.

jokes.text: Do you believe in me? / I believe you.
jokes.setup: Andy, as 'Older Male Lab Assistant Number One,' asks Darryl for moral support before the eyewash
jokes.punchline: Darryl says 'I believe you' — not 'I believe IN you,' which Andy asked for, but a subtly different phrase that confirms Andy's existence rather than his potential
jokes.explanation: Beautifully subtle. Andy asks 'Do you believe in me?' (a plea for faith in his ability/potential). Darryl responds 'I believe you' — confirming Andy exists and is telling the truth, which is the minimum possible form of belief. It's both dismissive and accidental, and Darryl's total disinterest makes it perfect. Great economy — the difference of one word is the entire joke.

jokes.text: Damn it! God... Sorry. Yeah, I'm fine. I'm fine. Okay. I got mad. Yeah. 'Cause I don't like losing, Pete. I'm just gonna... Sorry, I'm mad, Pete. I'm mad. I'm really mad. I wanted to win. We were gonna win a lot of money. I was gonna buy you a sweater.
jokes.setup: Erin loses in the semifinals and has a breakdown in front of Pete
jokes.punchline: Her breakdown culminates in 'I was gonna buy you a sweater' — after escalating rage about losing $2,000, the promised gift is a sweater, which is an absurdly modest ambition for the money
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to Erin's competitive arc. The escalating 'I'm mad, Pete. I'm mad. I'm really mad.' is funny repetition, and 'I was gonna buy you a sweater' is the perfect deflation. Out of $2,000, a sweater is what she was planning — sweet, sad, and funny.

jokes.text: Well, you know how much I appreciate the opportunity to hang out with your mom more, so let me just put this in my calendar. / I acknowledge with gratitude that you are being kind and responsible enough to include it in your calendar. / Thank you. Your mom is a treasure.
jokes.setup: Pam tells Jim about a dinner obligation; Jim responds in therapy-speak
jokes.punchline: Jim uses 'opportunity' sarcastically for an obligation he didn't choose; Pam's response is so formal it parodies its own therapeutic intent; 'Your mom is a treasure' is delivered with performed sincerity
jokes.explanation: The therapy-speak gag is running its course here. Still functional but less sharp than earlier deployments. 'Your mom is a treasure' as performed sincerity is the best beat.

jokes.text: Jim takes a phone call mid-therapy homework conversation; Pam calls it out; Jim says 'I appreciate the sacrifice' sarcastically
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are having a genuine feelings conversation using therapy language; Jim's phone rings and he takes it
jokes.punchline: Pam calls him out; Jim says 'I appreciate the sacrifice' with clear sarcasm; Pam: 'That was a little sarcastic'
jokes.explanation: This iteration of the running gag works better because it now has genuine conflict underneath it. Jim using therapy language sarcastically shows the exercise has completely broken down. The 'I think that's a little unfair' / 'Really? I've been putting the kids to bed by myself every night for months' escalation gives the comedy real emotional weight.

jokes.text: I've been putting the kids to bed by myself every night for months. And you had to miss one phone call. Is that your truth, Jim? That's really your truth? / I guess I will swallow my truth.
jokes.setup: Real marital conflict surfaces through the therapy-speak framing
jokes.punchline: 'I guess I will swallow my truth' — Jim uses the therapeutic language to announce he's backing down, which is both a surrender and a darkly funny misuse of the framework
jokes.explanation: 'Swallow my truth' is a great phrase — it's the opposite of the therapy's intent (speak your truth), and Jim deploys it with resigned awareness. The humor and pathos are blended here, which is classic late-era Office.

jokes.text: Are you guys high? Because, if so, to speak my truth, I would appreciate the sacrifice of including me in some hits off your kind buds.
jokes.setup: Kevin wanders into Jim and Pam's tense therapy-speak conversation
jokes.punchline: Kevin immediately adopts their therapeutic language to request marijuana — using 'speak my truth,' 'appreciate,' and 'sacrifice' in service of bumming weed
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Kevin's interruption perfectly crystallizes why the therapy-speak sounds so strange to outside ears, and his instant adoption of all three terms ('speak my truth,' 'appreciate the sacrifice') to request drugs is character comedy at its best. The phrase 'hits off your kind buds' in therapeutic framing is inspired. Kevin has no idea he's walked into a real marital moment — he just wants weed and has found a new framework for asking. Best deployment of the therapy-speak running gag.

jokes.text: The Mark 47 is ready for launch.
jokes.setup: Dwight prepares his paper airplane for the semifinals
jokes.punchline: He has named his paper airplane 'The Mark 47' and refers to its throwing as a 'launch,' treating a paper airplane with military precision naming conventions
jokes.explanation: Very Dwight — he's named his paper airplane with a military designation and treats throwing it as a launch. Character integration is high; it's a small but perfectly formed joke.

jokes.text: Pam: 'I wish we'd started this exercise six months ago. My heart just feels so... Blocked up.'
jokes.setup: After Kevin's interruption, Pam tries to return to sincere emotional processing
jokes.punchline: 'Blocked up' — after all the elevated therapy vocabulary, her honest emotional expression lands on a word that's more constipation than emotion
jokes.explanation: The joke is that after all the therapy jargon, when Pam tries to speak genuinely, the word she reaches for ('blocked up') is inadvertently funny — clinical, slightly gross, and not quite right emotionally. It also has a ring of truth: her feelings are constipated. Nice deflation of the emotional scene.

jokes.text: Kevin's paper airplane 'The Mark 47' launch — with 'Less paste' instruction
jokes.setup: Kevin is still trying to make a flyable plane despite being eliminated
jokes.punchline: He's named his plane 'The Mark 47' (implying 46 prior failures) and someone tells him to use 'less paste' — he's using paste on a paper airplane
jokes.explanation: Two-for-one joke: 'Mark 47' implies Kevin has tried 46 times and is now numbering his attempts with aerospace-project naming conventions; and he's using paste on a paper airplane, which would make it worse, not better. The 'less paste' note is said casually as if this is a known issue. Both details are specific and very Kevin.

jokes.text: We want you to win. Dwight told me about your situation. It's such a pity. Just use the money wisely. Okay?
jokes.setup: Nellie approaches Angela mid-competition to explain why they're rooting for her
jokes.punchline: Nellie's 'pity' speech during the competition is deeply condescending — 'it's such a pity,' 'use the money wisely' — and delivered with complete sincerity, making it worse
jokes.explanation: Cringe comedy through oblivious condescension. 'Use the money wisely' to a proud woman like Angela is the worst thing Nellie could say, and she says it warmly. The gap between Nellie's kindness and Angela's likely reaction is the comedy.

jokes.text: I know a guy who can turn that into $800. Hint, it's me.
jokes.setup: Dwight has won $2,000 in the paper airplane contest
jokes.punchline: Kevin offers to convert $2,000 into $800 — a dramatic loss — as if this is a service; the 'hint, it's me' clarification implies Kevin regularly does this and considers it a skill
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The premise — Kevin offering to convert money into less money as a service — is brilliantly absurd. 'Hint, it's me' is the perfect economy touch; it implies Kevin has a reputation as a money-converter (downward), which he seems proud of. The gap between 'I know a guy' (implying specialized expertise) and 'I can turn $2,000 into $800' (financial destruction) is the heart of the joke. Highly quotable, excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Well, I guess you needed the money more than me, huh? Use it wisely.
jokes.setup: Dwight has just deliberately lost the final to Angela but won't admit it
jokes.punchline: Dwight's fake-magnanimous 'I guess you needed it more' maintains the fiction of fair competition while 'use it wisely' echoes Nellie's condescending advice — but from Dwight it's simultaneously a cover story and genuine care
jokes.explanation: The callback to Nellie's 'use it wisely' gives Dwight's line extra dimension — he's accidentally echoing the condescension Nellie showed, while his true motivation is genuine love. The irony is multi-layered.

jokes.text: I was disappointed in Dwight today. He showed a weakness that was unbecoming. Even if he did do it for me. I don't need pity, and I don't need charity. I have my dignity, and that's enough.
jokes.setup: Angela gives a talking head about Dwight throwing the match for her
jokes.punchline: Angela's wounded pride — criticizing Dwight's romantic gesture as 'weakness' and 'unbecoming' — while simultaneously acknowledging 'even if he did do it for me' reveals she's touched but won't admit it
jokes.explanation: Angela's self-defeating pride is very in-character — she can't accept the gesture without criticizing it. The humor is in the contorted logic: she's criticizing the person who loves her for loving her too obviously. Understated character comedy.

tmdb_overview: Dwight and Angela participate in a paper airplane contest and compete against each other. Meanwhile, Andy prepares for a potential acting job, and Jim and Pam utilize new skills.
